chunks: Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Mahbub, from al-'Abbas, from 'Ali ibn Mahziyar, from Fadalah ibn Ayyub, from Musa ibn Bakr, from Zurarah, who said:

I heard Abu Ja'far عليه السلام forbidding silk clothing for men and women, except that which is of silk mixed with khazz, such that its weft or its warp is khazz, or linen, or cotton. Rather, it is only pure silk that is disliked for men and women.

key_terms.الْحَرِيرِ: silk clothing material discussed in the ruling
key_terms.الْمَحْضُ: pure, unmixed, referring here to pure silk
key_terms.خَزٍّ: khazz, a textile used here as a blending material with silk
key_terms.سَدَاهُ: its warp, the other principal thread direction in woven cloth
key_terms.قُطْنٌ: cotton, mentioned as a permissible material mixed with silk
key_terms.كَتَّانٌ: linen, mentioned as a permissible material mixed with silk
key_terms.لَحْمَتُهُ: its weft, one of the two principal thread directions in woven cloth
key_terms.مَخْلُوطٍ: mixed or blended with another material

ai.seo_question: Is praying in pure silk disliked, and does the ruling differ for mixed silk fabric?
ai.summary: This hadith reports that Abu Ja'far عليه السلام forbade wearing silk for men and women, while exempting fabric in which silk is mixed with other materials such as khazz, linen, or cotton. The ruling specifically concerns pure silk, indicating a legal distinction between unmixed silk and blended textiles in the context of prayer and dress.
